newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ'S BOLGER DOES NOT RULE OUT APPROACH TO DUNNE.
newsitem.headline: NZ'S BOLGER DOES NOT RULE OUT APPROACH TO DUNNE.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Thursday refused to rule out appointing a minister from a party outside the coalition, despite sacked Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton saying his vote for the government was assured.
Asked if he ruled out appointing lone United MP Peter Dunne to replace Kirton in the executive, Bolger told Reuters: "At the moment I am not ruling anybody in or out."
There has been speculation the government would offer Dunne a ministerial position to shore up its one seat majority.
Bolger said he had had no discussions with Dunne.
Dunne told reporters he was not disappointed by Kirton staying with NZ First, but he said the decision was not the end of the matter.
"Time will tell. I think this is a fluid situation.
"I think this is just part of an on-going process and to this extent nothing has changed," he said.
Asked if he would be happy taking Kirton's former Customs portfolio Dunne said that was leaping a long way ahead and he had not yet received a call from the Prime Minister.
Bolger said he expected Kirton would cooperate now.
"It would be rather foolish to just stay in there to be an irritant so I have to presume that he is staying in the NZ First caucus to make a constructive contribution."
He said any further attacks on himself by Neil Kirton would be "unfortunate".
"I would hope that the focus now can be on implementing the coalition's health policy," Bolger said.
He said the stability of the government had never been threatened.

"We were stable. There was no instability. A member was sacked from his associate health portfolio and that didn't in any way destabilise the government in any shape or form. He has now decided to stay in his caucus. That is that."
Bolger said he and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters had had brief discussions on the possibility of filling the slot created by Kirton's removal.

"But we haven't taken that through to any finality. There is no absolute urgency in that but I certainly do need another associate minister of health; the job is bigger than one minister," Bolger said.
